components.body: Decide whether one quantity is greater than, less than, or equal to another.
You already know how to count a group and say how many things it has.
If two groups sit side by side, the one that runs out first has fewer. The one still going has more. If they end together, they are equal.
Line up counters in two rows and match them one to one.
components.accessible_text: Two rows of dots. The top row has five dots; the bottom row has three. The top row is longer, so five is greater than three.

components.body: We write greater-than as >, less-than as <, and equal as =. The open side of > and < faces the larger number.
Compare 5 and 3. Match them up: 5 has two extra. So 5 > 3. Check: the open side faces 5, the larger number.
Compare 4 and 7 together. Which runs out first?
Write the correct symbol between 8 and 6.
Match groups one to one. More, fewer, or equal — then use >, <, or =.
Tomorrow, compare two two-digit numbers without drawing counters.
Understand that a digit's position gives it a value of ones, tens, hundreds, and so on.
The same digit means different amounts depending on where it sits. In 30, the 3 means three tens; in 3, it means three ones.
Break down 42. The 4 is in the tens place, so it is 40. The 2 is in the ones place, so it is 2. 42 = 40 + 2.
A digit's place tells you its value: ones, tens, hundreds.
